caption: Hi, I'm Aarav. This is a story about an apartment that held fifty-two degrees at seven in the morning, eleven mornings in a row.

The tenant's landlord stopped answering in January. What the tenant didn't know is that the city already had a file on the building: 2315 Barnes Avenue in the Bronx, 102 open class C violations, the oldest open for 601 days.
Heatline is a shared case page for a tenant and a legal aid advocate. Each of them gets their own agent, on the same page, with different tools.
The data is New York's own housing enforcement record: HPD violations, complaints, 311 heat calls, and owner registrations, pulled by SODA query with the exact URL kept beside every number.
Here is the tenant's window. The agent calls building violation history with no arguments and reads the record straight off the case. 102 open class C. 601 days.

The tenant says: no heat again, fifty-two degrees at seven. Match condition to code returns section 27-2029, the heat rule, 68 degrees from six in the morning to ten at night. Log condition fires. A card asks the tenant to confirm. A person clicks it, not the agent.

Now the advocate's window, same case. Nine tools. Assemble HP action packet and request evidence are here. File packet and log condition are not. The server checks the same thing on every write, so a forged call gets a 403.
The advocate's agent asks the tenant for a photo of the thermostat. It lands in the tenant's window without a reload.
Then it assembles the packet: parties from the registration, conditions with their code sections, the building record, the timeline, relief sought. Confirm.
Back in the tenant's window, the agent calls file packet. One draft waiting. Confirm. Filed.
Last, the 311 complaint. It's a declarative WebMCP form. The agent fills every field. Only a human presses Send.
No chatbot wrapper can do this, because nothing else knows which window is asking. The page declares its own tools, the roles are capability keys, and every write goes through a person.
The city's own record was always public. Now the tenant's agent can read it, and the advocate's agent can build the case from it. That's Heatline.
